title: Find the Letter
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
panel: Find the LetterSay each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 10).Say and look for: Say: Here are twelve letter cards from the treasure chest. I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter. Say: Point to the letter q. (top row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter N. (bottom row, first card) Say: Point to the letter h. (top row, second card) Say: Point to the letter F. (bottom row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter y. (bottom row, second card) Say: Point to the letter D. (top row, first card) Say: Point to the letter l. (bottom row, sixth card) Say: Point to the letter G. (top row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter j. (bottom row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter P. (top row, third card) The top row reads D, h, P, q, G, w and the bottom row reads N, y, U, j, F, l. Six cards are uppercase and six are lowercase, and two of the twelve are never asked for. This is the direction the standard asks for: the child hears a name and finds the printed letter. Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. q, j and y all hang below the line, and lowercase l is a plain upright stroke. If the child points to the wrong one of those, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. A child sitting right at that goal gets about 6 of these 10, which the suggested rating reads as approaching. Count the uppercase and the lowercase separately, hold each against the number above, and set the rating yourself.

title: Uppercase Letters
dir: Say the name of each letter.
panel: Uppercase LettersShow one letter at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each letter the student gets right, then type the number right in the box for this part.Letters: S, M, A, T, R, B, O, C, P, N, E, L, D, F, H, I, G, K, U, W, J, Y, V, Z, Q, XNotes for you: Show one letter at a time and ask: What is this letter? Mark each letter the student names correctly. Give no hints and do not say the sound. A name said slowly still counts. Write down every letter that was missed. Which letters they are matters more than the total. If the student misses five in a row, stop this part and move on. Record what was reached. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. The two inventories are scored under one code, so a child right at goal lands near 33 of 52 and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Hold the uppercase count and the lowercase count against the two numbers above and set the rating yourself.

title: First Sounds

Say: Fish. What is the first sound in fish? (/f/) Point to the boat. Say: Boat. What is the first sound in boat? (/b/) The answer is the sound, not the letter name. title: Rhyme Time

title: Slow Parrot
dir: Listen to the slow parrot talk. Say the whole word.
panel: Slow ParrotRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Say and look for: Say: Pip the parrot talks very slowly. Put the parts together and tell me the word. The pictures can help you. (The pictures are not in the same order as the words.) Say with a pause between the parts: tur ... tle. (turtle) Say: ba ... na ... na. (banana) Say the two sounds: /k/ ... /ee/. (key) Say the three sounds: /m/ ... /a/ ... /p/. (map) The first two are syllables. The last two are single sounds. Note which kind the child can blend.

title: Pip and the Key
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: Pip the parrot found a shiny gold key on the beach. She flew to the big rock, but the key did not open anything there. Next, she flew to the tall palm tree and saw a little wooden box. (Stop here. Ask what Pip will do next.) Pip put the key in the box and turned it. Click! The box opened, and inside were crunchy seeds for Pip and her friends.Say and look for: Read the story out loud. Stop after the third sentence, when Pip sees the little box. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Pip will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like try the key in the box or open the box.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What did Pip find on the beach? (Pip the parrot. A gold key.) Ask: Where did Pip go first? Where did Pip go after that? What was inside the box? (First the big rock, then the palm tree. Seeds were in the box.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. Count the last question correct when the two places are in the right order.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sea Turtle Facts
dir: Listen to your teacher read about sea turtles. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: Sea turtles live in the ocean. They have flippers that help them swim. A mother sea turtle crawls onto the beach at night. She digs a hole in the sand and lays her eggs in it. Then she covers the eggs with sand and goes back to the sea. When the babies hatch, they crawl to the water.Say and look for: Read the facts out loud. If picture supports are on, the child can look at the picture while listening. Ask: Why do you think the mother turtle covers her eggs with sand? (A reason that makes sense: to hide them, to keep them safe, or to keep them warm. The text does not say why, so the child has to figure it out.) Ask: What other animals do you know that lay eggs? (Uses what the child already knows: birds, chickens, ducks, frogs, fish, snakes, lizards.) Say: What do you want to know about sea turtles? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or How. (Asks a real question about sea turtles. Telling a fact is not asking a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sound Letters

Say: Tiger starts with /t/. Write the letter for /t/. (t or T) A letter counts when you can tell what it is. Backward or wobbly letters still count. Uppercase or lowercase is fine. You give the sound. The child picks and writes the letter. If an adult names the letter for the child, do not count that one.

Look for: the child tells you what the writing says, like It says gold. This shows the letters stand for a word or an idea. If the child writes only a name, that is a fine start. title: Name It

title: Mystery Chest
dir: Something is hiding in the chest. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
panel: Mystery ChestRead the directions aloud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Your secret: a banana is hiding in the chest. Answer each question in a few words: It is yellow. You can eat it. It is a fruit. You peel it. It is long and curved. Look for: asks a real question to get information (not only a guess, like A ball!). Look for: asks a follow-up question that builds on your answer (after You can eat it, asks Is it a fruit? or Is it sweet?). Look for: checks the idea with a question at the end (Is it a banana?). If the child is stuck after 4 or 5 questions, give one more clue.

What would you see? Look for: 2 or more details in the description.

title: Count the Treasure
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one over to the side as you count it out loud. (One number word for each thing moved, no skips and no double counts. Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) Those first two counts are the evidence for this standard, because they are the ones you can see for yourself. The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. Say: Point to each shell on your screen and count out loud. (6 shells) Look for one number word for each shell, with no skips and no double counts. Say: Now count the gems. (10 gems) Say: Now count the gold coins. (13 coins, in rows of 5, 5, and 3) On the screen rows, have the child say the numbers slowly enough that you can hear one number word for each picture, and watch the child's eyes move along the row. Where you cannot tell, leave the row out of the count rather than taking an adult's word for it. Count an item correct only when the last number said matches the number of objects. Note where the count broke down: skipped a number, counted one twice, or lost track after 10.Then fill in the counts below.

End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. A child sitting exactly at that goal still lands near 60 percent of whatever sample you show, and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Set the rating yourself against those two counts.

title: Read the Fable

text: Four lines from the ship log. Line What it says 1 Sailors crossed this ocean in wooden ships with cloth sails, hundreds of years ago. 2 Yesterday the crew drew a new map of the cove. 3 People found their way at sea by the stars, long before there were maps like ours. 4 This morning a crew member checked the weather on the radio. How do we know about the sailors of long ago? Four kinds of thing tell us. An artifact is an object they left behind, like a brass compass in a museum case. A photograph shows what something really looked like. An interview is what you learn by asking somebody who was there, or whose family was. A document is something written down at the time, like a ship log or a letter. All four of those are primary sources. A book somebody wrote later, after reading the logs, is a secondary source.
qs: Which two lines tell about things that happened long ago?
Which two tell about things that happened in the last day or two?
Things that come straight from the time you are studying are called primary sources. Name two of the four kinds listed, and say which kind a ship log is.

Name two of the four kinds listed, and say which kind a ship log is.Answer: Any two of: an artifact, a photograph, an interview, a document. A ship log is a document, and it is a primary source. Both parts are what is being checked. A student who can also say that a book written later is a secondary source has the whole of this part. (HSS-2.1)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about her. Answer out loud.
text: Sally Ride loved science. She loved to find out how things worked. She trained hard. In 1983 she became the first. She was the first American woman to fly up. She went into space. She rode a spacecraft around the Earth. She ran science tests while she was up there. People had said it for a long time. This was a job for men only. After she came back she taught. She spent years teaching science to young people. She wrote books for them. She wanted girls to know something. They could do this work too.
qs: What did Sally Ride do that no American woman had done before?

title: How an Apple Grows
dir: Listen to your teacher read about apple trees. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: Every apple starts out as a flower. In the spring, an apple tree is covered with white flowers. A bee lands on a flower to drink. Yellow dust called pollen sticks to the bee's legs. The bee carries that pollen to the next flower, and that is the job the flower was waiting for. Then the petals fall off and a tiny green apple starts to grow where the flower was. The apple grows all summer long. By fall it is big and red and ready to pick.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the three pictures first. Say: This is the order an apple grows in. First a flower, then a bee, then an apple. Then read the facts out loud. Ask: What if no bees at all came to the orchard in the spring? What do you think would happen? (Not many apples would grow, or no apples would grow. The facts never say this part, so the child has to put two of them together.) Ask: Have you ever seen a bee on a flower, or watched a bug land on a plant? Tell me about it. (Any real answer from the child's own life counts.) Say: What do you want to know about apple trees? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or Why. (Asks a real question about trees, flowers, bees or apples. Telling a fact instead of asking is not a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Count the Rows
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
panel: Count the RowsRead the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 6).Say and look for: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one over to the side as you count it out loud. (One number word for each thing moved, no skips and no double counts. Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) Those first two counts are the evidence for this standard, because they are the ones you can see for yourself. The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. There are two lines of them. (12 baskets, in lines of 6 and 6) Row 3. Say: Now count the honey jars. There are two lines of them. (13 honey jars, in lines of 7 and 6) Row 4. Say: Now count the flowers. There are two lines of them. (14 flowers, in lines of 7 and 7) Count an item correct only when the last number said matches the number of objects. title: Name the Letter
dir: Say the name of each letter.
panel: Name the LetterShow one letter at a time with the Next and Back buttons. The arrow keys work too.Keep track of each letter the student reads correctly, then type the number right in the box for this part.Letters, in order: P, C, L, H, D, N, F, W, G, J, c, p, w, kNotes for you: Say: Let's pick letters off the apple tree. Tell me the name of each letter. Click Next after each one. Correct means the child says the letter name. If the child gives the sound, ask once: What is the name of this letter? The first 10 are uppercase (P C L H D N F W G J). The last 4 are lowercase (c p w k). Write down the ones missed. These are different letters from the LP 1 game. Use both lists together to see how many letter names the child knows so far. If the child misses 4 in a row, stop and change the number tried. Find the Letter at the top of this stop is the part this standard is written for. The standard asks the child to match a spoken name to its printed form, and naming a letter on sight is harder than that, so rate this standard on the Find the Letter count and keep this deck as the extra note. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. A child sitting exactly at that goal still lands near 60 percent of whatever sample you show, and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Set the rating yourself against those two counts.

Everyone who works at the stand got one slip of paper and wrote down the kind they wanted. Then they counted the slips out loud so that everybody could see the count. Red apples got nine slips. Green apples got seven. Yellow apples got four. Red and green went on the table. When every single person votes on the thing itself, that is called direct democracy. A whole town has too many people for that, so the people of a town vote for a few helpers, called a council, and the council makes the rules. That is called representative democracy.Everyone got a slip of paper and a say in the choice. Is that a right or a responsibility?Answer: A right. title: Read the Story
dir: Read the story out loud. Use your best reading voice.
text: Nell and Omar went to the orchard on Saturday morning. The grass was still wet. Nell wanted the biggest apple on the tree. But it was at the very top. She jumped. She could not reach it. Omar shook the branch. The apple did not fall. Then Nell saw a ladder by the barn. Omar held it still while she went up step by step. At last she picked the big red apple. She did not eat it. She gave it to Farmer Jo, who makes the best pie in town.

title: Tree Stump Tale
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the fable. Then tell it back in your own words and answer out loud.
text: Squirrel and Hedgehog Squirrel and Hedgehog each had a pile of apples to take home before dark. Hedgehog put two apples in his basket and set off down the path. “That is too slow,” said Squirrel. “I will carry all of mine at once!” He piled ten apples in his arms. Then he took three steps. Bump! The apples rolled down the hill and into the pond. Squirrel sat down and sighed. Hedgehog kept going, two by two. When the sun went down, all of his apples were safe at home. He gave half of them to Squirrel.

title: Buzzing Bees

text: Bees in the Orchard In spring, apple trees are covered with flowers. The flowers are white and pink. Bees fly from flower to flower. They drink sweet nectar. title: Rules, Money and the Stand
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the price list. Answer out loud.
text: The Saturday farm stand price list. What is on offer Price a basket of apples 60 cents a jar of honey 35 cents a loaf of bread 25 cents someone to carry your load to your car 10 cents Getting an apple from the tree to a kitchen takes a chain of people. The farmer grows and picks it. A processor washes, sorts and packs it at the packing shed, or presses it into juice. A distributor drives it in a truck to the stores. The weather decides how big the crop is, and the apples need good soil and plenty of water to grow at all. Long ago this chain was short. A family grew nearly all its own food in its own garden, kept a few animals, and ate what was ripe that month. Today most food travels a long way before anybody eats it, and a store has food from every season all year round.

title: Someone Who Made a Difference
dir: Listen to the story. Answer out loud.
text: Dr Martin Luther King Jr was a boy once. There were rules in many places then. They kept Black people and white people apart. Black children went to different schools. Black families had to sit at the back. It was the back of the bus. Dr King grew up to be a minister. He told people the rules were not fair. He asked everyone to change the rules without fighting. Thousands of people walked instead. They would not be riding the buses. They kept it up for more than a year. In the end the rule was gone. It was about the back of the bus. In 1963 he stood in Washington. He told a huge crowd about his dream. Children would be judged by who they are. It is who they are inside. The rules did change. We remember him on a holiday. It comes every January.
qs: What did Dr King think was not fair?
What did he ask people to do instead of fighting?
Name one way what he did made a difference to other people.
panel: Read the directions aloud. Then read the text on the screen aloud, once, and again if the student asks. Then read each question, one at a time.The student answers out loud.Keep track of which answers are right, then type the number right in the box for this part (out of 3).What did Dr King think was not fair?Answer: The rules that kept Black people and white people apart. Any of the examples counts: different schools, having to sit at the back of the bus.What did he ask people to do instead of fighting?Answer: Change the rules in a peaceful way. Walking instead of riding the buses is the example in the passage. Accept speaking up, marching, or telling people it was wrong.Name one way what he did made a difference to other people.Answer: The unfair rules changed, Black families no longer had to sit at the back of the bus, children could go to school together, and we remember him on a holiday. title: Nib’s Morning

In his tree home, next to the pumpkin patch.) Ask: Nib went to three places. Where did he go first? Next? Last? (First the hay bale, next the sunflowers, last the big pumpkin.) title: How a Pumpkin Grows
dir: Listen to your teacher read about pumpkins. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: Here are some true things about pumpkins. A pumpkin starts as a seed. In the spring a farmer plants the seed in the dirt. Rain and sunshine help the seed. A long green vine grows along the ground. Yellow flowers open on the vine, and a tiny green pumpkin grows where each flower was. All summer long the pumpkin gets bigger, and then it turns orange. In the fall it is ready to pick. Inside every pumpkin there are new seeds.Say and look for: Read the facts out loud. If picture supports are on, point to the three cards first and say: Card 1 is a seed. Card 2 is a little sprout coming up. Card 3 is a pumpkin growing on the vine. Then read the facts. (The farmer will plant them and new vines and new pumpkins will grow. The facts do not say this part, so the child has to put two of them together.) Ask: Have you ever planted a seed or helped something grow? Tell me about it. (Uses what the child already knows: a bean in a cup, a garden, a flower, a tree at home. Any real answer from the child's own life counts.) Say: What do you want to know about pumpkins? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or Why. (Asks a real question about pumpkins, seeds, vines, or the farm. Telling a fact instead of asking is not a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Rows on the Vine

Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) The standard asks the child to match a spoken name to its printed form, and naming a letter on sight is harder than that, so rate this standard on the Find the Letter count and keep this deck as the extra note. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. A child sitting exactly at that goal still lands near 60 percent of whatever sample you show, and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Set the rating yourself against those two counts.

title: Barn Door Tale

text: Goat and the Bag of Seeds Goat found a bag of sunflower seeds by the fence. Hen had dropped it on her way home. Goat’s tummy growled. “No one saw me find it,” he thought. He looked at the seeds for a long time. Then he walked all the way to Hen’s coop and knocked. “Is this your bag?” he asked. Hen clapped her wings. “Yes! Those seeds are for my chicks.” She poured some into Goat’s hat to say thank you. Goat walked home feeling full and glad, even before he ate a single seed.

(bottom row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter B. (top row, third card) The top row reads S, a, B, e, M, o and the bottom row reads R, u, V, k, T, j. Six cards are uppercase and six are lowercase, and two of the twelve are never asked for. This is the direction the standard asks for: the child hears a name and finds the printed letter. Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. a, e and o are all small and round, so they are the ones to watch, and j is the one letter on the cards that hangs below the line. If the child points to the wrong one of that group, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of them. A child sitting right at that goal gets about 6 of these 10, which the suggested rating reads as approaching. Count the uppercase and the lowercase separately, hold each against the number above, and set the rating yourself.

(cocoa) Say: snow ... flake. (snowflake) Say the two sounds: /i/ ... /s/, with a long i. (ice) Say the three sounds: /s/ ... /u/ ... /n/. (sun) The first two are syllables. The last two are single sounds. Note which kind the child can blend.

title: The Lost Mitten
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: The Lost Mitten
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: Tess the fox lives in a village where cold white snow covers the ground all winter. One morning Tess pulled on her two red mittens and walked out to go skating on the frozen pond. First she stopped at the old stone well to look at the ice inside it. Then she stopped under the tall pine tree and shook the snow off her tail. When Tess got to the pond, one mitten was gone! (Stop here. Ask what Tess will do next.) Tess walked back along her own footprints. There in the snow under the tall pine tree was her red mitten. She pulled it on and skated all afternoon.Say and look for: Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after one mitten is gone. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Tess will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like go back and look for it, or walk to the pine tree.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What did Tess pull on before she went out? (Tess the fox. Her two red mittens.) Ask: Where did Tess stop first? Where did she stop after that? (First the old stone well, then the tall pine tree.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. Count the last question correct when both places are named in the right order.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Snowshoe Hares
dir: Listen to your teacher read about snowshoe hares. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: A snowshoe hare is an animal that looks like a big rabbit. It lives where snow covers the ground all winter. Snow is cold and white and soft. In the summer the hare has brown fur. When winter comes, its fur grows in white instead. A snowshoe hare also has very big back feet. The big flat feet spread out on top of the snow, so the hare walks on the snow instead of sinking down into it.Say and look for: Read the facts out loud. If picture supports are on, the child can look at the two pictures while listening. Point to the brown hare on the grass and then the white hare on the snow. Ask: Why do you think white fur helps the hare in the winter? (A reason that makes sense: a white animal is hard to see on white snow, so it can hide from animals that hunt it. The text does not say why, so the child has to figure it out.) Ask: What do you wear or do to keep warm when it is cold outside? (Uses what the child already knows: a coat, mittens, a hat, boots, a blanket, stay inside, drink something warm.) Say: What do you want to know about snowshoe hares? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or How. (Asks a real question about hares. Telling a fact is not asking a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

title: Sound Letters

Say: Fire starts with /f/. Write the letter that makes the /f/ sound. Hold it up. (f or F) Point to the lamp. Say: Lamp starts with /l/. Write the letter for /l/. (l or L) Point to the nose. Say: Nose starts with /n/. Write the letter for /n/. (n or N) A letter counts when you can tell what it is. Backward or wobbly letters still count. Uppercase or lowercase is fine. You give the sound. The child picks and writes the letter. If an adult names the letter for the child, do not count that one.

title: Label Your Snow Day
dir: Draw one thing you would see on a snowy day. Write letters to tell what it is. Hold it up.
panel: Label Your Snow DayThe student needs paper and a pencil.Read the directions aloud.Ask the student to hold their paper up to the camera so you can see the working, not only the answer.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Say: Snow is cold and white and it covers the ground. Draw one thing you would see on a snowy day. It can be a sled, a mitten, a tree, or anything you like. Then write a word or some letters to tell what it is. Hold it up and tell me what you wrote. Look for: writing that is separate from the drawing (letters or marks that look like letters, not only a picture). Look for: 2 or more letters you can recognize. They do not need to spell the word. Look for: the child tells you what the writing says, like It says sled. This shows the letters stand for a word or an idea. If the child has never seen snow, any cold weather picture works. If the child writes only a name, that is a fine start. Ask: What does it say? Then ask for some letters about the drawing too.

title: Name It
dir: Look at each picture. Answer out loud.

Say: What is this? (a cabin, a house, or a home) Picture 2. Say: What is this? (a snowman) Picture 3. Say: What is this? (yarn, wool, or string. This is a harder word.) Picture 4. Say: What is this person doing? (skiing) Picture 5. Say: What is this person doing? (snowboarding, or riding a board) Picture 6. Say: This is a cube of ice. Tell me two words about what ice is like. (Describing words such as cold, hard, slippery, wet, smooth, clear, freezing.) Pictures 1 to 3 are naming words, 4 and 5 are action words, and 6 is describing words. Note which kind was hard.

title: Mystery Crate
dir: Something is hiding in the crate. Ask your teacher questions to find out what it is.
panel: Mystery CrateRead the directions aloud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Say and look for: Your secret: a pine cone is hiding in the crate. Do not tell. Say: Something from the woods is hiding in my crate. Ask me questions to find out what it is. You can ask things like: Is it an animal? What color is it? Answer each question in a few words: It is brown. It is bumpy. It is not an animal. It fell off a tree. A squirrel likes to carry it away. It comes from a pine tree. Look for: asks a real question to get information (not only a guess, like A rock!). Look for: asks a follow-up question that builds on your answer (after It fell off a tree, asks What tree? or Is it a leaf?). Look for: checks the idea with a question at the end (Is it a pine cone?). If the child is stuck after 4 or 5 questions, give one more clue.

title: Would You Rather
dir: Pick one. Tell your teacher why.

Would you rather ride a sled down a snowy hill or skate on the frozen pond? Tell me which one and why. Look for: tells an opinion (picks one). Look for: gives a reason that explains the pick. If there is no reason, ask once: Why? Say: Tell me more. Who would go with you? What would it feel like? Look for: 2 or more details in the description.

title: Snowball Count
dir: First count some small things from near you. Then count the pictures on the screen.
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Start with real things, before the screen. Say: Go and get ten small things you can hold, like spoons, blocks, socks or crayons, and set them on the table where I can see them. Then say: Move each one over to the side as you count it out loud. (One number word for each thing moved, no skips and no double counts. Moving each object is what makes the matching visible to you, so watch the hands as well as the numbers.) Say: Push them back into a pile, add a few more, and count the whole lot again the same way. (Any number past ten. The goal is 10 or more with one number word for each object. If the count breaks down partway, write down the number it broke at.) Those first two counts are the evidence for this standard, because they are the ones you can see for yourself. The screen rows below are still worth doing and they show whether a count holds together over bigger groups, but the child is pointing at a monitor you cannot see, so do not rate this standard on them alone and do not rate it on what an adult in the room reports. Say: Point to each mitten on your screen and count out loud. (11 mittens, in rows of 6 and 5) Look for one number word for each mitten, with no skips and no double counts. Say: Now count the pine trees. (10 trees in one row) Say: Now count the snowballs. Snowballs are balls of packed snow. (14 snowballs, in rows of 5, 5, and 4) On the screen rows, have the child say the numbers slowly enough that you can hear one number word for each picture, and watch the child's eyes move along the row. Where you cannot tell, leave the row out of the count rather than taking an adult's word for it. Count an item correct only when the last number said matches the number of objects. Note where the count broke down: skipped a number, counted one twice, or lost track after 10.Then fill in the counts below.

In the bottom box the deer are spread out, so their row looks longer. Look for counting, not guessing from how long the row is. Listen for the words more, same, fewer, or less.

title: Name the Letter

Tell me the name of each letter. Click Next after each one. Correct means the child says the letter name. If the child gives the sound instead, ask once: What is the name of this letter? The first 10 are uppercase (H N P I L D G W C F). The last 6 are lowercase (n i p l d c). Write down the ones missed. Watch for uppercase I called lowercase l, and for lowercase d called b. Those two mix-ups are common and worth a note. End of TK goal: about 15 to 20 uppercase and 12 to 16 lowercase letter names. Find the Letter at the top of this stop is the part this standard is written for. The standard asks the child to match a spoken name to its printed form, and naming a letter on sight is harder than that, so rate this standard on the Find the Letter count and keep this deck as the extra note. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. Those are counts of letters, not a share of any deck. A child sitting exactly at that goal still lands near 60 percent of whatever sample you show, and the suggested rating reads that as approaching. Set the rating yourself against those two counts.

What is the first sound? (/b/) Now point to the letter that makes that sound. (b) Row 4. Point to the sled. Say: Sled. What is the first sound? (/s/) Now point to the letter that makes that sound. title: Write in the Cabin

text: Write a letter to Hare. Should she have asked Badger for help sooner? Tell her why, using the story. Write 3 or 4 sentences. Start with: Dear Hare End with: Your friend and your name Look back at the story Deep snow covered the path to the pine woods. Hare wanted to visit her friend Badger. But the snow came up to her ears. She hopped and hopped and got nowhere. “I can do it myself,” she puffed. Then she sat down, tired and cold. At that time people could be bought and sold. They were sold as property. It happened in part of the country. Lincoln believed that was wrong. He worked to end it. He signed a paper. title: Find the Letter

I will say a letter name. Point to the card with that letter. Say: Point to the letter q. (top row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter N. (top row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter i. (top row, second card) Say: Point to the letter c. (bottom row, sixth card) Say: Point to the letter P. (bottom row, first card) Say: Point to the letter l. (bottom row, fourth card) Say: Point to the letter D. (top row, first card) Say: Point to the letter y. (bottom row, second card) Say: Point to the letter F. (bottom row, fifth card) Say: Point to the letter G. (top row, third card) The top row reads D, i, G, q, N, z and the bottom row reads P, y, U, l, F, c. Six cards are uppercase and six are lowercase, and two of the twelve are never asked for. This is the direction the standard asks for: the child hears a name and finds the printed letter. Keep the uppercase and the lowercase results apart in your notes. i and l are both thin and tall, and q and y both hang below the line. If the child points to the wrong one of a pair, write down which one. End of TK goal for this standard: match about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase letters and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase. title: Pip and the Flags
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Pip and the Flags
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Read aloud to the student: Pip is a Weddell seal. Seals like Pip live on the ice at the bottom of the world, and her fur is smooth and grey. One morning Pip pushed herself along the snow with her front flippers, past the little flags that the science team put in the snow to mark their trail. First she passed the weather station, a tall pole with three little cups on top that spin in the wind. Next she passed three green tents. Then she came to a stack of wooden crates beside the frozen sea. (Stop here. Ask what Pip will do next.) Pip sniffed the crates and smelled fish. She pulled one dried fish out of an open crate and carried it in her mouth all the way back to her hole in the ice.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: A science team is camping on the snow. They push little flags into the snow so they can find their way. The tall pole with cups on top, on the left, is a weather station. It tells them how hard the wind is blowing. The grey animal in front is a seal. Seals swim in the cold sea here and rest on top of the snow and ice. Point to the stack of crates, with one crate open. Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Pip comes to the stack of crates. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Pip will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like look in the crates, open one, climb up, or find food.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? What color is her fur? (Pip the Weddell seal. Grey.) Ask: Pip passed three things. What did she pass first? Next? Last? (First the weather station, next the three green tents, last the stack of crates.) Count it correct when all three are in the right order. Ask: What did Pip find in the crate? What did she do with it? (A dried fish. She carried it back to her hole in the ice.) If picture supports are on, the picture on the screen can help the child remember. The weather station, the three tents and the crates are in the same order as the story, left to right.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Crate Labels
dir: Listen to your teacher. Point to the letter on your screen.
panel: Say each prompt listed below out loud, exactly as written, one at a time.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 5).Say and look for: Say: Every crate has a small letter painted on it. I will say a letter name. Point to the crate with that letter. Say: Point to the letter d. (second crate from the left) Say: Point to the letter w. (last crate on the right) Say: Point to the letter b. (first crate on the left) Say: Point to the letter g. (fourth crate from the left) Say: Point to the letter h. (fifth crate from the left) The crates read b, d, p, g, h, w from left to right. This is the other direction from the flag letters: here the child hears the name and finds the printed letter. b, d and p look alike. If the child points to the wrong one of those three, write down which one. That mix-up is common at this age. This stop and Find the Letter in stop 1 are scored under the same code, so their counts add together. The TK goal is a count of letters, about 15 to 20 of the 26 uppercase and about 12 to 16 of the 26 lowercase, and a child sitting right at that goal lands near 60 percent of any sample. Set the rating yourself against those two counts rather than taking the suggested one.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Dot Jumps In
dir: Listen to the story. Then answer out loud.
text: Dot Jumps In
panel: Read the directions aloud.The student answers out loud.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 4).Read aloud to the student: Dot is a young penguin. Penguins live at the bottom of the world, where the sea is cold and full of ice. Penguins cannot fly, but they can swim very fast. Dot wanted to swim, but she had never been in the water before. Her mother stood beside her on the ice. A friend was already in the water. The friend swam in a circle, calling up to her. Dot stood on the edge of the ice floe, a flat piece of ice that floats on the sea, and looked down at the water. (Stop here. Ask what Dot will do next.) Dot took a big breath and jumped in. The cold water made her blink. Then she swam two fast circles around her friend and climbed back up onto the ice.Say and look for: If picture supports are on, point to the picture before you read. Say: This flat piece of ice floating on the sea is called an ice floe. Penguins rest on it and jump off it to swim. The small grey penguin at the edge is Dot. The big penguin beside her is her mother. The penguin swimming in the water is Dot's friend. Read the story out loud. Stop at the bold note, right after Dot looks down at the water. Ask at the stopping place: What do you think Dot will do next? (Any guess that fits the story, like jump in, swim, or wait a little longer.) Then read the rest. Ask: Who is this story about? Where is she standing? (Dot, a young penguin. On the edge of the ice floe.) Ask: What did Dot want to do? What was hard about it? (She wanted to swim. She had never been in the water before.) Ask: Tell me what Dot did at the end, in order. (She jumped in, then she swam two circles around her friend, then she climbed back up onto the ice.) Count it correct when the jumping comes before the swimming and the climbing out comes last. Penguins live at the bottom of the world, where the sea is cold and full of ice. The seals and the whales in this game live there too.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Seal Holes
dir: Listen to your teacher read about seals. Then answer out loud.
panel: Read the text marked "Read aloud to the student" below at a steady pace. Read it a second time if the student asks.Then ask the questions listed below.Tick each check below as you see it, then type the number met in the box for this part (out of 3).Read aloud to the student: A seal is an animal that lives in the cold sea near the ice. Seals swim under the water to catch fish to eat. But a seal breathes air, just like you do. Where the sea is coldest, the top of the water freezes into a thick lid of ice. So a seal uses its sharp front teeth to scrape a round hole in that ice. The seal swims up through the hole, pokes its nose out, and takes a breath. Then it dives back down to look for more fish.Say and look for: Read the facts out loud. If picture supports are on, point to the pictures first and follow the arrows. Say: The seal swims under the ice near some fish. Next it scrapes the ice with its front teeth. Next it pokes its head up through the round hole. Next it takes a breath. Last it dives back down. Then read the facts. Ask: Why is that hole so important to the seal? What would happen if the hole froze shut? (The seal breathes air, so it has to come up to the top for a breath. With the hole frozen shut it could not get air under the thick ice, so it would have to scrape a new hole or find another one. The text does not say this part, so the child has to put two facts together.) Ask: You breathe air too. What do you do when you are under the water and you need a breath? (Uses what the child already knows: come up to the top, put my head out, stand up, hold my nose. Any real answer from the child's own experience counts.) Say: What do you want to know about seals? Ask me a question. You can start with What, Where, or How. (Asks a real question about seals. Telling a fact instead of asking is not a question.)Then fill in the counts below.

Say: Crate starts with /k/. Write the letter for /k/. (c or C. The letter k also counts, because it stands for the same sound.) Point to the goggles. Say: These are goggles. They keep the wind and the bright snow out of your eyes. Goggles starts with /g/. Write the letter for /g/. (g or G) A letter counts when you can tell what it is. Backward or wobbly letters still count. Uppercase or lowercase is fine. You give the sound. The child picks and writes the letter. If an adult names the letter for the child, do not count that one.Then fill in the counts below.

title: Radio Check

Look for: asks a question about which bag or which tent (there are three tents and two bags). If the child does not ask, prompt once: Do you know which one I mean? Then answer: The red bag. The tent next to the flag. Message 2. Say: We leave in the morning. Pack food for the trip. Look for: asks a question about how much or how long, like How many days? or How much food? Then answer: Pack food for three days. Look for: a follow-up question that builds on your answer, like Do we need water too? or How much food for one day? Answer it in a few words. Look for: says the plan back to you to make sure, like So the red bag and food for three days? If the child does not, ask: Can you tell me back what you will do? Look for: asks a real question to get information (not only a guess, like A fish!). Look for: asks a follow-up question that builds on your answer (after You look through it, asks What do you see? or Is it for your eyes?).
